metadata.title: The Test You Did Not Design.
metadata.playlist: Computational Skepticism for AI — Deep Explainers
metadata.purpose: deep-explainer of Bear's skepticism.ai essay 'The Test You Did Not Design' — three structural limits, Turing/Searle, the override that must be real, the authority to refuse
metadata.source: skepticism.ai — Nik Bear Brown, 'The Limits of AI: What the Tools Cannot Do — The Test You Did Not Design' (Apr 28, 2026); full text pasted into the Cowork session 2026-09-02 and preserved in SOURCES.md

metadata.description_blurb: A clinical system passed every test its engineers designed and still harmed three patients. Liam, in for Bear, takes apart why: three limits that scaling cannot fix — meaning, intentionality, and the gap between data and world — what Turing and Searle actually settle, where the limits bite, why the override has to be real, and why the authority to refuse is the most important authority in the system.
chapters: The Test You Did Not Design
Act I: The Sequence Is the Argument
Act II: Three Limits Scaling Cannot Fix
Act IV: Where the Limits Bite

Act VI: What the Work Looks Like

beats.act: cold open
beats.narration_text: Hallo — this is Liam, in for Bear. Here's a system that passed every test its engineers gave it. Ninety-four percent accuracy. Every internal review threshold met. Regulatory submission cleared. Fairness within tolerance. Three patients harmed within six months. Not fraud. Not recklessness. The tests were real. They were tests for a question the harm never asked — and nobody had been trained to ask whether the scope was the problem.

beats.act: ACT II — Three Limits Scaling Cannot Fix
beats.narration_text: Act two. Three limits — not problems waiting on a bigger model, but features of what these systems are.

beats.act: ACT II — Three Limits Scaling Cannot Fix
beats.narration_text: Meaning. Intentionality. The gap between data and world. These are not failure modes that better tooling eventually closes. They're constitutive — part of what an AI system is. More data, more compute, and every one of them is still standing exactly where it was.

beats.act: ACT II — Three Limits Scaling Cannot Fix
beats.narration_text: The first limit is meaning. The system processes symbols. The symbols have referents in the world. The system has no representation of the referents — it manipulates the symbols, and the meaning is supplied by whoever reads the output. When the two pictures align, everything looks fine. When they diverge, the user is still reading a statement about the world.

beats.act: ACT II — Three Limits Scaling Cannot Fix
beats.narration_text: You can hear the objection: large multimodal models pick up something like meaning from embeddings and grounding. It's a serious objection, and it doesn't need settling. Whether these models have meaning is genuinely open. Whether an engineer can assume they do before a clinical deployment is not.

beats.act: ACT II — Three Limits Scaling Cannot Fix
beats.narration_text: The second limit is intentionality — the philosopher's word for aboutness. When you say the kettle is on, your words point at a particular kettle in a particular kitchen. And you are the one doing the pointing.

beats.act: ACT II — Three Limits Scaling Cannot Fix
beats.narration_text: The system's outputs lack that stable directedness. Run the same system in two contexts and users read the outputs as being about different things. Its aboutness tracks the user's reading, not a directedness of its own. So someone has to supply the pointing — and that someone is the human supervisor.

beats.act: ACT II — Three Limits Scaling Cannot Fix
beats.narration_text: The third limit is the one I'm most certain of. The data is always less than the world — a sample, captured by particular instruments, under particular conditions, with particular exclusions. Competence is over the data, not the world. Generalization holds inside a distribution and fails at its boundary — and the boundary is where systems fail.

beats.act: ACT III — Two Famous Arguments
beats.narration_text: Act three. Two famous arguments, and what each one actually shows.

beats.act: ACT III — Two Famous Arguments
beats.narration_text: Turing, nineteen-fifty. If a machine can convincingly imitate a human in conversation, on what principled basis would you deny it intelligence? We don't demand more than behavioral evidence from other humans. It settles a methodological question — and that is all it settles.

beats.act: ACT III — Two Famous Arguments
beats.narration_text: The test is over behavior. The limits are about what stands behind behavior. Turing knew that — it was a proposal about method, not a claim about metaphysics. The people who cite him as proving that imitation is intelligence credit him with a stronger claim than he made.

left.note: Behavior is legitimate evidence — no double standard for machines.

right.label: Does not settle
right.note: Meaning, intentionality, or competence over the world.

beats.act: ACT III — Two Famous Arguments
beats.narration_text: Searle, nineteen-eighty, runs the reverse. A person following symbol-manipulation rules can produce output indistinguishable from a Chinese speaker's, without understanding a word. So behavior consistent with understanding does not entail understanding. Symbol manipulation is not understanding.

beats.act: ACT III — Two Famous Arguments
beats.narration_text: What the Chinese Room does not settle is whether contemporary systems are doing only symbol manipulation — whether embeddings, attention, and multimodal grounding add up to something more. It's a strong constraint on shallow accounts of meaning. Not a deep constraint on current architectures. Same overclaim, opposite direction.

right.note: Whether today's architectures are only symbol manipulation.

beats.act: ACT III — Two Famous Arguments
beats.narration_text: Together they produce a workable stance. Behavior is testable evidence — take it seriously. And behavior is not the whole of understanding. Both moves at once. Only test behavior and you miss the limits. Only invoke the limits and you skip the testing. The discomfort of holding both is the method working.

beats.act: ACT IV — Where the Limits Bite
beats.narration_text: Act four. Not every deployment is equally exposed — so where, exactly, do the limits bite?
beats.new_visual_element: Act card — Where the Limits Bite

shot.motion_claim: act card: title springs in, hairline draws under it on the act number, holds for the act name

beats.act: ACT IV — Where the Limits Bite
beats.narration_text: A system classifying product images on a manufacturing line lives where the limits barely matter: the context is well specified, the data-world gap is small and monitorable, a human supplies the meaning. There, skepticism is methodology. Clinical recommendations, vehicle decisions, judicial risk scores, agents in shared spaces — there, apparent competence outruns the real thing, and the supervisor's skepticism is the safety mechanism.

beats.act: ACT IV — Where the Limits Bite
beats.narration_text: This is what 'this specific patient' looks like. Not a category — a person, on a particular day, with a history the training data never held. The clinician has to have the time, and the standing, to disagree with the screen. That is the practice. Not the disclaimer.

beats.act: ACT IV — Where the Limits Bite
beats.narration_text: The engineering response is specific. Specify, in writing, what the system can be tested for and what it cannot. Put the limits in the documentation as a primary product, not fine print, so a regulator can see what the validation warrants. Keep humans where the limits bite. And build the override so it is real.

beats.act: ACT IV — Where the Limits Bite
beats.narration_text: What that looks like on the page: a limits section that names the three, says which question the validation answered, and states what makes a human override possible — time, standing, legibility. An override that is documented but practically impossible is not an override. It's a fiction.

props.title: validation-report.md — §7 Limits
props.code:
## 7. Limits (primary product — read before §3 Results)

ANSWERED:      "Does this case match a training category?"
NOT ANSWERED:  "What is going on with this specific patient?"

Structural limits (not closable by more data or compute):
  MEANING         referents supplied by the reader, not the model
  INTENTIONALITY  no stable directedness across sites
  DATA ≠ WORLD    competence is over the sample; boundary unmonitored

Human override — REQUIRED at each bite point, and REAL:
  time        minutes to disagree, not seconds
  standing    disagreement is normal, not an escalation
  legibility  the recommendation shows what it was scoped to

Verdict: PROCEED | MODIFY | DEFER | REFUSE  (refusal is on the menu)

beats.act: ACT V — The Authority to Say No
beats.narration_text: Act five. The authority that matters most — and the one most deployments quietly assume away.
beats.new_visual_element: Act card — The Authority to Say No

shot.motion_claim: act card: title springs in, hairline draws under it on the act number, holds for the act name

beats.act: ACT V — The Authority to Say No
beats.narration_text: There are deployments where, given the stakes, the limits are a reason not to deploy at all. The supervisor's authority to refuse is, structurally, the most important authority in the system. And most deployments don't preserve it. The validator is hired to validate. Clearance is expected. Refusal is assumed away.

right.label: What that removes
right.note: The option to refuse — exactly when it matters most.

shot.motion_claim: the two columns land on their spoken clauses; the spark line is the judgment

beats.act: ACT V — The Authority to Say No
beats.narration_text: The case against refusal calls itself realism. The business case is made, procurement is done, the announcement is scheduled, and stopping is politically expensive. That reality deserves respect. Then ask what it means to build a process where the option to say no is gone at the moment it's most needed.

beats.act: ACT V — The Authority to Say No
beats.narration_text: So ask the limit case. At what level of stakes does an engineer's obligation to refuse become binding, whatever the institutional pressure? The clinical system that harmed three patients is an answer. The risk score behind an unjust sentence is an answer. The vehicle that killed someone is an answer. These are the forms the limits take when the override is fictional.

beats.act: ACT V — The Authority to Say No
beats.narration_text: A validation practice that cannot accommodate refusal is not a safety practice. It's documentation of a deployment that was going to happen regardless. The calibration work, the bias analysis, the governance structures — all of it becomes elaborate cover if the option to stop is not real.

beats.act: ACT VI — What the Work Looks Like
beats.narration_text: Most engineers spend their careers stating ninety percent confidence on questions where their actual hit rate sits well below it. They don't know this. Nobody runs the experiment on them. That gap — between the confidence you state and the confidence you've earned — is the thing the practice exists to close.

beats.act: ACT VI — What the Work Looks Like
beats.narration_text: The practice isn't a methodology you learn once. It's the repeated act of stopping. Locking the prediction before you look. Asking what the data is actually evidence of. Saying out loud what you don't know. Built over years, through small acts of epistemic honesty — and it changes what you ask before a deployment goes live, not after.

beats.act: ACT VI — What the Work Looks Like
beats.narration_text: The system passed every test. The engineers designed the wrong tests. Three patients were harmed. That isn't history — it's the structure of the next failure: cleared every review, in a context the data didn't reach, on a question the framework wasn't scoped to. The person who recognizes the gap, has the authority to act, and uses both — that's the professional the field needs.

beats.act: verdict
beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Three limits that capability scaling doesn't touch: meaning, intentionality, and the gap between data and world. Failures cluster at the boundary, where the data stopped and the world didn't. Turing and Searle each settle less than they're quoted for — behavior is evidence, and behavior isn't the whole. Where the limits bite, the supervisor's skepticism is the safety mechanism, the override has to be real, and the authority to refuse is the one that matters most. A validation practice that cannot say no is not a safety practice.

beats.act: your turn handoff
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — paste it into Claude. It reads: Take one AI deployment I actually know — from my work or the news. Before any analysis, make me lock a prediction: which of the three limits — meaning, intentionality, or the data–world gap — bites hardest here, and what failure it would produce. Then write the limits section of its validation report: what the tests answered, what they could not, and where a human override must be real. Finish by telling me whether you would proceed, modify, defer, or refuse — and what would change your mind. End quote. Two checks. The lock has to come before the analysis — if Claude analyzes first and predicts after, make it start over; the lock is the discipline. And if the limits section reads like a disclaimer, it failed — it should name the question the tests did not answer. Run it on a deployment you'd have to answer for. Liam, in for Bear.
